lignes.texte: If you stacked loan on top of loan every month, just to survive,
the bank would cut you off. They’d seize your assets. They’d ruin your life.
But when the US government does it… they call it fiscal policy.
Right now, America burns through almost $3 billion of taxpayer money every single
day. That money doesn’t fund anything. It just pays off the interest on debt.
The government is stuck in an economic death spiral
now and they’re scrambling for an escape route…
Your bank account.
For 15 years, the Federal Reserve had the U.S. economy hooked up to a financial IV.
Free money was pumped into the system constantly. Interest rates were so low
people were bragging about remortgaging their homes. It was like getting a lottery win.
And Washington got in on the act.
In 2021, the country’s debt had hit $28 trillion, but no one was worried. The
average interest rate was sitting at a low 1.5%, so borrowing cash felt like a cheat
code. The entire year's interest payment was $352 billion. For a superpower, it was pocket money.
Everyone thought the good times would continue,
so the borrowing continued. Debt was stacked on top of debt.
By 2022, the national debt passed $30 trillion for the first time.
The pandemic blew a hole in the budget. As small businesses and critical infrastructure struggled
to stay afloat, the government had to act. The handouts worked, stopping an economic collapse,
but the terms the government borrowed that cash on caused the real damage.
Every time Washington borrows money, it comes with a timeframe. Money can be locked in at a
fixed rate for 30 years, just like a mortgage. Or it can be a short term,
fast loan that can be due in months. When the bill lands, they just borrow again to cover it.
The fast money was cheaper. So that’s what Washington took… in huge amounts.
It works like a mortgage with a teaser rate. Your payment is small for 2 years.
Then it resets to whatever the market says. Millions of Americans took that
deal before the 2008 crash, and many of them lost their homes.
Washington took the same deal… for the whole country.
Nobody stopped it. Politicians don’t win elections
by slashing budgets. Instead, the country gambled on interest rates staying low… forever.
They didn’t.
The economy caught fire.
Prices skyrocketed. Millions of ordinary Americans saw their household bills surge
out of control. By June 2022, prices were rising at 9.1% a year. To stop the
whole thing from burning to the ground, the Federal Reserve did the only thing it could.
It raised interest rates.
Over the course of 16 months, the rates increased by more than 5 full
points. It was the fastest rise in 40 years. Price hikes began to slow,
but the move hurt the country. All that cheap, short term pandemic debt is due and there’s no
cash to cover it. That means the Treasury has to print and sell new bonds to make the payment.
Except it’s not that easy.
That 1.5% rate doesn’t exist anymore. Today’s investors want more. 4% to be
exact. And they get it. And that adds more to the bill. In 2019,
servicing the national debt cost the government $375 billion. By July 2026, it was $963 billion.
The interest payments are close to $1 trillion.
Interest is now the second biggest thing the government spends money
on. Only Social Security beats it. It’s more than the cost of
the Department of Defense and Homeland Security… combined.
Right now, the interest bill steals nearly
20 cents of every single dollar the government collects from taxpayers.
Split that across the entire population and every American covers roughly $3,000 a year.
Economists will say a country like America can carry debt forever because it prints
the world’s reserve economy. And for decades, they were right.
But eventually, that plan catches up with you.
When it comes to clearing debt, the government doesn’t pay off old bonds with cash. It auctions
off fresh ones to somebody else. In 2025, the Treasury held 444 auctions,
about 9 every week. Each one puts a set amount of new debt up for sale. If plenty of buyers turn up,
the government borrows cheaply. But if the buyers don’t show up,
the government has to lure them in somehow. To convince someone to buy that debt, the government
is forced to hike the interest rate. That rate gets added to the national debt for years.
There’s no announcement. No front page headlines. You’re just expected to deal with the fallout.
The total amount of debt maturing in 2026 stands at $9.6 trillion. And the
Treasury has to find a buyer for every single dollar. If it doesn’t, the government runs out
of cash to cover things like pensions, military payrolls and medical coverage.
Treasury officials call this kind of short term borrowing their financial shock absorber. It
used to make up a fraction of the nation’s debt, around 15%. Today, it’s closer to 25%, the highest
since the 2008 crash. That means a quarter of America’s debt is exposed to brutal market forces.
They can’t just lock it into 30 year fixed bonds. Dumping that amount of debt all at once,
would cause the market to crash. Interest rates would explode. So they’re trapped.
Loans that were agreed when money was practically free, now they are at the mercy of the market.
And when Washington has to pay more, so does everybody else.
Including you.
Between 2021 and 2023, mortgage rates jumped from about 2.65% to nearly 7.8%. On a $400,000 loan,
that’s roughly $1,300 more every month. All because the government’s borrowing costs moved.
It’s almost like taking a cash advance on a new credit card to pay the minimum payment on
an old one. Your total debt doesn’t shrink, but the interest rates go up. That’s what the U.S.
government is doing. It’s borrowing hundreds of billions to cover the interest on the old debt.
In August 2026, the national debt crossed $40 trillion. America has borrowed as much
in the last 10 years than it did in its first 2 centuries combined. Even if the
government cancelled every single program, scaled back the military
and sent the entire federal workforce home tomorrow, it would change a thing.
The interest contacts are legally binding. The cash has to come from
somewhere. And that demand is creating friction.
On one side you’ve got the Treasury. It desperately needs cheap money to refinance
the debt. Skipping a payment would be catastrophic for the American economy.
On the other side is the Federal Reserve. Its job is to keep your grocery bill under control.
To stop inflation, the Fed is refusing to cut rates. It’s a
necessary sacrifice that it feels it has to make.
Neither side can give the other what it wants without committing self-sabotage.
If interest rates remain high, the refinancing of debt continues at crippling prices. The interest
payments add up, until the spiral out of control and everything comes crashing to the ground. The
second option sees the Fed aggressively cutting rates and printing more dollars to buy up the
bonds no one wants. But it also obliterates the purchasing power of the money in your wallet.
There’s no third option. That’s the dilemma America is facing.
Government analysts expect the annual interest bill to reach $2.1 trillion a
year by 2036. That’s roughly double where it stands now. And if interest rates rise
one point higher than forecast, another $3.2 trillion is added to the bill over the decade.
Essentially, the government is relying on buyers snapping up the debt.
But they’re backing away.
Right now Japan is the biggest foreign holder, sitting on $1.14 trillion of
American government debt. The yen has been under strain, and to protect its collapsing currency,
Tokyo is selling off American bonds for cash. Britain sits second on that list and has been
dealing with the effects of a post Brexit world, while China has spent years trimming its holdings.
Every time a foreign power dumps American bonds, the price gets pushed down further.
And every time, Washington is forced to hike the interest
rates. And the bill that lands on the Treasury’s desk gets bigger.
When foreign buyers step back, that debt doesn’t
disappear. It gets soaked up closer to home, by American banks, funds,
and savers. This ties even more of your money to the government’s ability to keep paying.
Meanwhile, the gap keeps widening while everyone argues over how to
solve the problem. The government spent $432 billion more than it collected in July 2026.
That was the fourth worst month in the country’s history. It
came up $1.8 trillion short over the first 10 months of the budget year.
Investor and founder of the hedge fund Bridgewater, Ray Dalio made a successful
career from analysing the market. He spent 40 years betting on which countries pay their bill
and now he’s looking at America’s tab. He says this ends with a heart attack brought on by debt.
But America has been here before.
In April 1942, the U.S. was 4 months into a war it had to pay for. The Treasury needed
to borrow more money than anyone ever had in human history. There wasn’t a market on
earth that was large enough to lend as cheaply as America wanted. Left alone,
interest rates would have climbed until the war itself was out of reach.
So the Fed agreed to hold short government borrowing at three-eighths of 1%. It also capped
the rate on long bonds at 2.5%. On paper it was just a technical arrangement between 2 agencies.
Whatever the market wanted, that was the price people got. When sellers pushed rates up,
the Fed just printed money to buy bonds until they fell again. It worked exactly
as designed. The war got paid for, and it was ordinary families who put up the money.
When the war ended, the government didn’t realise the shackles. The
interest rate caps stayed on for 6 more years. Nobody in power
wanted to hand the Treasury a higher bill. So the ceiling never came off.
And that decision crushed the families who had bought into the war effort and
snapped up the bonds. Prices skyrocketed by 17.6% in a single year. Those war
bonds were still locked at their wartime rate, and the money inside them shrank.
Technically no one defaulted. The government paid back every single bond in full, right on schedule.
But they paid it back in dollars that bought a fraction of what they used to.
Say your grandfather bought a bond in 1943, sold to him at a school hall or a factory gate. He
wanted to do his bit and help pay for the landings in Normandy. He held it for 10 years. He trusted
the system. And he received every cent he was promised. But by the time he got his money back,
those cents couldn’t buy a house, a car or the future he’d spent a decade planning for.
Nobody who bought a bond was told.
Behind the scenes, the Fed spent years trying to break the agreement. By January 1951,
prices were climbing again, so President Truman called the whole committee to the White House
and told them to keep the caps in place. He wanted cheap debt and didn’t care about the consequences.
The Fed refused.
They fought back.
It took until March 1951 for the Fed to win back the right to set rates
on its own. But by the time it won that bureaucratic battle, American savers had
already been wiped out. It’s the same playbook politicians use today. Because it’s the only
form of bankruptcy where nobody has to stand behind a podium and utter the word default.
Critics will argue that history proves the debt not as bad as it seems. America came out
of World War II owing way more than the country produced in a year. It held that massive amount
of debt for decades and managed to climb out the financial hole without a catastrophic collapse.
And it’s true.
But they ignore the fact that America had help. It was saved by the baby boom. The economy had
a post-war manufacturing boost and a younger workforce. It was a golden era for the economy.
Today, that is completely reversed. The workforce is aging rapidly, birth rates are declining,
and the government's spending seems to be on autopilot. And you just have to accept it. There’s
not going to be a public vote on the national debt. It’ll happen behind closed doors, in rooms
you’ll never have access to. The only time you’ll realize it is at the local store or the gas pump.
Buying power is reduced, money doesn’t go as far and savings lose their value on a daily basis.
When you shrink the dollar, you shrink the promise.
Your bank balance remains the same, but the world moves a little further out of reach.
People who have land, stocks or commercial property will be able to ride it out.
But the millions of families who hold raw dollars are the ones who feel the
effect. Investors are already seeing the warning signs. They’re cashing
out and moving their money into gold or other resources that hold their value.
The debt works out to about $117,000 for every person in this country. Roughly $297,000 for
every household. Nobody signed up for it. It was borrowed in your name while you were at work,
one auction at a time, on a schedule that never stops. It never asks for your permission.
Politicians don’t care about your tax bracket. They don’t care about the zeros in your bank
account. All they care about is that the system survives. And to do that,
fresh money has to arrive before the old promises come due.
The interest rate time bomb is already going off. The timer has hit zero. Your
hard earned dollars are the only thing left to pay it with. The economic machine is
insatiable. It will keep feeding until there's nothing of real value left in your account.
The system can’t be fixed. It can’t be voted out. And it won’t spare you.
There's no version of this where you don't pay for America’s debt.
